procedural_history.originating_court: Single Judge of the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Gwalior
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgement dated 24th January, 2018, passed by the Division Bench of the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Gwalior.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Single Judge passed an order on 17th November, 2017, in a writ petition. The State Government appealed this order to the Division Bench of the High Court. The Division Bench dismissed the State Government's appeal on 24th January, 2018.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State Government appealed the Division Bench's judgement to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashing the Division Bench's judgment and upholding the Single Judge's order.

directions: The judgement dated 17th November, 2017, passed by the learned Single Judge is upheld.
The impugned judgment dated 24th January, 2018, passed by the Division Bench of the High Court is quashed and set aside.
Parties are left to bear their own costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellants have erred in rejecting the candidature of the respondent to the post of Constable, despite the latter having truthfully disclosed in his aﬃdavit the fact that he had faced trial in a criminal case which had resulted in his acquittal.

facts: The respondent applied for the post of Constable and was selected after qualifying in the required examinations.
In the verification form, the respondent truthfully disclosed that he had been involved in a criminal case which had resulted in his acquittal.
The criminal case involved serious, non-compoundable offenses, including charges under the POCSO Act, which are considered to involve moral turpitude.
The respondent was acquitted because the prosecution could not prove the case 'beyond doubt', and a compromise was reached with the complainant for some of the charges.
Based on this, the appellants (the State) rejected his candidature, deeming him unsuitable for the post.
law: An employer has the discretion to consider the antecedents of a candidate to determine their suitability for a post, especially for a disciplined force like the police which requires impeccable character.
Mere acquittal in a criminal case does not automatically entitle a candidate to an appointment.
Even when a candidate makes a truthful disclosure, the employer is entitled to examine the nature of the offense and the nature of the acquittal.
A distinction is made between an 'honourable' or 'clean' acquittal and an acquittal based on the benefit of the doubt or technical reasons.
The employer's decision should not be interfered with unless it is found to be arbitrary or mala fide.
application: The Court acknowledged that the respondent had made a candid disclosure and had not suppressed any information.
However, the Court focused on the employer's right to assess the respondent's suitability.

It examined the trial court's judgment and determined that the acquittal was not 'clean'. The acquittal was granted because the case was not proven 'beyond doubt' and was partly based on a compromise with the complainant.
The Court considered this to be an acquittal on the basis of 'benefit of doubt', not an honourable one.

Given the serious nature of the original charges (involving moral turpitude) and the high standards of character required for a police constable, the Court found that the employer's decision was justified.

The Court held that the State Government had judiciously exercised its discretion by considering all relevant factors, including the respondent's antecedents and the nature of the acquittal, to find him unsuitable for the post.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellants did not err in rejecting the respondent's candidature. Despite the truthful disclosure and acquittal, the employer was within its rights to assess the candidate's suitability. Since the acquittal was not 'clean' but was based on the benefit of the doubt for serious offenses involving moral turpitude, the employer's decision to deem the respondent unfit for the post of Constable was a valid and judicious exercise of its discretion.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellants have erred in rejecting the candidature of the respondent to the post of Constable, despite the latter having truthfully disclosed in his aﬃdavit the fact that he had faced trial in a criminal case which had resulted in his acquittal.
appellant_arguments: The decision to reject the respondent's candidature (or terminate his services) was a valid exercise of the Competent Authority's power and was not tainted by any mala fides or arbitrariness.
respondent_arguments: The rejection of his candidature was improper because he had been candid and made a full disclosure in his verification form about the criminal case in which he had been acquitted, and there were no other pending cases against him.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A decision directing the reinstatement of an employee is unsustainable when the employee has suppressed material facts or filed a false declaration.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Even if a candidate makes a truthful disclosure about a past criminal case that ended in an acquittal, the employer retains the discretion to examine the candidate's fitness. The employer is entitled to consider the nature of the original offense and the circumstances of the acquittal to determine if the candidate is of a suspect character or unfit for the post. If the employer concludes the candidate is unfit, particularly for a sensitive post in a uniformed service based on charges involving moral turpitude, it may reject the candidature.
legal_tests_applied: Even if a truthful disclosure has been made, the employer is well within its right to examine the fitness of a candidate and in a concluded criminal case, keep in mind the nature of the offence and verify whether the acquittal is honourable or benefit has been extended on technical reasons.
If the employer arrives at a conclusion that the incumbent is of a suspect character or unfit for the post, he may not be appointed or continued in service.
The yardstick to be applied has to depend upon the nature of post; higher post would involve more rigorous criteria for all services, not only to uniformed service.
The choice/option whether to continue or not to continue an employee based on their antecedents must be given to the employer.
policy_considerations: The question is not about whether an employee was involved in a dispute of trivial nature and whether he has been subsequently acquitted or not. The question is about the credibility and/or trustworthiness of such an employee.
An employer cannot be forced to continue an employee who... cannot be relied upon even in future.
Higher the post, more stringent ought to be the standards to be applied.
